# Introduction

[PLACEHOLDER — write after Sections 2-4 are done.]

The economic consequences of AI are the subject of intense debate. Leading AI executives predict rapid, large-scale displacement: Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, warns that AI could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within five years [@Amodei2026]; Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, told the United States Senate that AI will cause "significant change in labor markets," including substantial job displacement [@Altman2023]. Industry reports project that up to 300 million jobs worldwide are exposed to automation by generative AI [@BriggsKodnani2023]. On the other side, economists point out that automation has historically complemented labor before displacing it, creating new tasks that absorb displaced workers [@Autor2015; @AcemogluRestrepo2019]. Recent estimates suggest that AI's aggregate productivity gains may be far more modest than industry projections imply [@Acemoglu2025]. Both sides focus on the economic outcome --- how many jobs, how fast, at what wage. We ask a different question: what are the *political* consequences of these two economic scenarios? We show that the answer depends not on the magnitude of displacement but on its trajectory, and that the same trajectory stabilizes one type of political regime while destabilizing the other.

# The Logic of Crossed Fragility

Before the formalization in Section 3, we develop the logic verbally: why the same automation technology destabilizes one regime type while stabilizing the other, and why the pattern reverses when the trajectory changes.

## Automation trajectories and the structure of displacement

The model imports two stylized trajectories from the O-Ring automation framework [@GansGoldfarb2026]. Under task separability, tasks are independent: automating one does not affect the productivity of the others. If AI substitutes a sufficient share of tasks, the result is rapid displacement. Exposed workers lose their jobs, and the affected population experiences a uniform, shared loss. The displaced form a recognizable group with a common condition.

When tasks are quality complements, automation follows a different path. Automating some tasks raises the productivity of the remaining ones, because workers can concentrate on what has not yet been automated. Exposed workers become more productive, firms expand, and incomes rise, provided demand is sufficiently elastic. Some workers and sectors may still be negatively affected, but the aggregate experience of the exposed group is one of gain. At some point, AI capabilities cross a threshold and substitution begins. The key feature of this transition is its unevenness. The O-Ring structure means that some tasks are automated while others are not, some firms adopt faster than others, and some workers lose their jobs while others continue to benefit from complementarity. When displacement finally becomes widespread, the affected workers are not a homogeneous group experiencing a shared condition. They are scattered among firms still thriving and coworkers still gaining from AI-augmented productivity.

The final displacement of exposed workers is the same under both trajectories: all of them eventually lose their jobs. What differs is the structure of that displacement and the experience that precedes it. Under rapid automation, displacement is uniform and simultaneous; no exposed worker ever gained from AI. Under threshold automation, displacement is heterogeneous and dispersed among workers who benefited from the complementary phase --- some of whom were still gaining when others began to lose.

## Regimes and the selectorate

Democracies and autocracies differ in one fundamental respect: the size of the group that keeps the ruler in power --- the *selectorate* [@BuenoDeMesquita2003]. In a democracy, the ruler depends on a large coalition: voters, legislators, media, organized interests. In an autocracy, the ruler depends on a small coalition: generals, oligarchs, party leaders. From this single difference, three consequences follow.

*Information.* A ruler who depends on millions of people receives information from millions of sources --- a free press, open protests, independent statistics, parliamentary debates. A ruler who depends on twenty generals receives information from twenty generals --- who have every incentive to report that all is well. Democracy sees crises clearly; autocracy operates in a bubble. This is the dictator's dilemma [@Wintrobe1998; @EgorovGurievSonin2009]: the very repression that keeps the autocrat in power suppresses the information he would need to respond to threats. The democratic leader faces no such trade-off: protest is both the signal that reveals the crisis and the political demand that activates the response.

*Speed.* Convincing twenty generals is a meeting. Convincing a legislature is a process --- debate, committees, floor votes, regulatory implementation. Autocracy acts by decree; democracy acts by law. The law arrives, but it arrives late. This institutional lag is not a pathology but a structural feature of large-coalition governance: the same deliberative process that makes democracies responsive also makes them slow [@Tsebelis2002].

*Fiscal politics.* Compensating displaced workers costs money. The fiscal base is the economy as a whole --- taxes fall on everyone, regardless of regime type. But the *political authorization* to spend comes from the selectorate. In a democracy, the selectorate includes the voters: the same people who pay taxes are the ones who must approve spending. If the majority is not suffering, it blocks compensation at the ballot box. In an autocracy, the selectorate is a small elite that controls fiscal decisions over public resources. If the elite does not perceive a crisis, it will not authorize the ruler to spend --- and a ruler who diverts public funds without visible justification risks removal by the very coalition that sustains him [@Svolik2012]. The fiscal constraint is not about whose money it is, but about who has the political power to authorize its use.

These three consequences are not independent mechanisms bolted together; they are jointly derived from coalition size. A small selectorate produces poor information *and* fast decisions *and* elite fiscal control. A large selectorate produces good information *and* slow decisions *and* majoritarian fiscal politics. The model formalizes the informational consequence through a single regime-varying parameter --- the cost of protest $C_x$, where $C_A > C_D$. Institutional speed and fiscal authorization enter as separate regime-specific features of the model (Section 3).

## The four scenarios

The interaction between automation trajectories and regime characteristics produces four outcomes. Each regime's institutional advantage is activated by one type of crisis and rendered irrelevant by the other.

*Rapid displacement in a democracy --- stable.* The persistent, visible displacement generates protest. Workers who have lost their jobs take to the streets; workers who still have jobs but fear displacement support them. The protest serves as a signal: legislators see the crisis, the media covers it, and the political demand for compensation becomes irresistible. The legislature passes a compensation law. The law takes time --- legislation is slow --- but because the crisis is gradual and visible from the start, there is time. Compensation arrives before the regime is overwhelmed. The democracy's informational advantage is decisive: it sees the crisis early enough to act despite its institutional slowness.

*Rapid displacement in an autocracy --- falls.* The same crisis is moderate and persistent. The cost of protesting is high, so few workers take to the streets. The elite does not see the crisis: controlled media do not report it, internal assessments say all is well, and the small protests are too insignificant to alarm anyone. The autocrat cannot spend the elite's money on a crisis the elite does not perceive --- if he does, the elite removes him for incompetence. So the autocrat represses. Repression works in the short run. But displacement accumulates: workers who lose their jobs in one period remain unemployed in the next, and new workers are displaced each period. At some point, the accumulated volume of displaced workers generates protest that exceeds the regime's repressive capacity. By then, there is no compensation infrastructure in place, no institutional framework to absorb the shock. The regime falls. The autocracy's informational disadvantage is fatal: it cannot see the crisis building until it is too late.

*Threshold automation in a democracy --- falls.* During the complementary phase, most workers are prospering. AI augments their productivity, firms expand, incomes rise. The few who are displaced are scattered among beneficiaries with no grievance. There is no protest, because there is no widespread suffering. Without protest, there is no political signal. Without a signal, the legislature does not act. Crucially, the workers who are gaining from AI do not want to pay higher taxes to compensate the few who are losing --- the prosperity of the complementary phase actively blocks preventive investment in social insurance [@FinseraasNyhus2025; @DasguptaRamirez2025]. No compensation infrastructure is built during the good times. When AI crosses the threshold and displacement becomes massive and sudden, the democracy finally sees the crisis and acts --- but the law takes time. There is no standing infrastructure to deploy. Compensation arrives too late. The regime falls before the response can take effect. The democracy's institutional slowness is fatal precisely because its informational advantage was neutralized during the prosperity phase: there was nothing to see until it was too late to act.

*Threshold automation in an autocracy --- stable.* During the complementary phase, calm prevails --- no displacement, nothing to respond to. When the threshold is crossed, the displacement is so massive and sudden that it is impossible to ignore. GDP collapses, factories close, the crisis is visible even inside the elite's bubble. Unlike the moderate crisis of rapid displacement, which the elite could plausibly overlook, this shock is self-revealing: its sheer magnitude overwhelms the informational filters that normally insulate the autocratic selectorate. The elite sees the crisis and authorizes spending. The autocrat acts immediately --- by decree, without a legislature, without debate. Compensation arrives in the same period. Crisis resolved. The autocracy's speed advantage is decisive: when the crisis is large enough for everyone to see, the regime that acts fastest survives.

*The irony.* Each type of automation generates the type of crisis that exploits the weakness of the opposite regime. Moderate, persistent crises favor information --- whoever sees first can act in time. Massive, sudden crises favor speed --- when everyone finally sees, only the fastest responder survives. And the prosperity of the complementary phase is democracy's trap: it eliminates the political voice that would have activated the preventive response. The crossed fragility pattern is not a coincidence but a structural consequence of how selectorate size interacts with the temporal profile of economic disruption.
